posts.title: Hybrid Search: Fusing Keyword and Vector Retrieval with RRF
posts.subtitle: Vector search misses exact IDs and rare terms; keyword search misses paraphrases. Reciprocal Rank Fusion gets both without picking a winner.
posts.summary: Dense vector search is great at paraphrase but blind to exact tokens like IDs, codes, and rare terms; keyword search (BM25) is the mirror opposite. Hybrid search runs both retrievers and fuses their rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) — a simple formula that combines results by rank position instead of raw score, sidestepping the problem of comparing two incompatible scoring scales.

slides.title: Hybrid Search: Fusing Keyword and Vector Retrieval with RRF
slides.body: Pure vector search is great at paraphrase and bad at exact strings — a part number, an error code, a name it's never seen. Pure keyword search is the opposite. Hybrid search runs both and fuses the rankings instead of picking one.

slides.title: Embeddings Don't Preserve Exact Tokens
slides.body: A dense embedding compresses a chunk of text into a few hundred numbers optimized for semantic similarity — and in doing so, it can blur exactly the details a keyword match would nail.
bullets: Query 'error E1234' can rank a chunk about generic error handling above the one chunk that literally contains 'E1234', because embedding space cares about topic, not substring identity
Rare tokens — product SKUs, legal citations, function names, ticket IDs — are often undertrained in the embedding model, so their vectors don't reliably separate from similar-looking text
BM25 (classic keyword search) has the opposite failure: it can't tell 'car' and 'automobile' are related, so a paraphrased query returns nothing

slides.title: Run Both Retrievers, Then Fuse the Rankings
slides.body: Hybrid search doesn't pick BM25 or vector search — it runs both against the same query, gets two independently-ranked lists, and merges them into one ranking.
bullets: The hard part isn't running two retrievers, it's combining their scores: BM25 produces unbounded term-frequency statistics, cosine similarity is bounded [-1,1] — averaging them directly compares incompatible units
Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) sidesteps that entirely by ignoring raw scores and fusing on RANK POSITION instead
It needs no score normalization, no retraining, and no per-query calibration — just each retriever's ordered list

slides.title: Why Fuse by Rank, Not by Score
slides.body: RRF's key trick: it never touches the actual BM25 or cosine score, only each result's position in its own list, which makes it robust to differently-scaled or differently-distributed retrievers.
bullets: Formula: RRF(d) = the sum, over every retriever that returned d, of 1 / (k + rank(d)) — 0 contribution from a retriever that didn't return d at all
k is a constant (commonly 60, from the original 2009 Cormack/Clarke/Buettcher paper) that flattens the curve so rank 1 vs. rank 2 matters far more than rank 50 vs. rank 51
Because it needs no calibration, RRF is the default fusion method in most hybrid search implementations rather than a learned re-scorer

slides.title: Fusing Results for "Why does error E1234 happen?"
slides.body: Two retrievers, two very different rankings for the same query. Only fusion gets the answer right.
bullets: Chunk A ('Generic error-handling guide', no literal 'E1234'): vector rank #1 (topically closest), BM25 rank #47 (barely matches on the word 'error')
Chunk B ('E1234: cache eviction race condition', contains the literal string): vector rank #9 (embedding buried it), BM25 rank #1 (exact token match)
Chunk B wins the fused ranking — the answer neither retriever alone put first, but that both retrievers found worth returning at all

slides.title: BM25 vs. Vector vs. Hybrid: Know the Tradeoff
slides.body: Neither single retriever wins outright — that's exactly why hybrid pipelines run both instead of picking a favorite.

slides.title: Where Hybrid Search Still Falls Short
slides.body: Hybrid search fixes a retrieval-method mismatch, not every RAG failure mode.
bullets: It doubles retrieval infra and latency: you're maintaining and querying an inverted index AND an ANN index, plus a fusion step, not just one
Choosing k in RRF matters less than people expect for overall ranking, but a very small k over-weights whichever retriever happens to rank something #1, even on a fluke
It can't fix bad chunking or a stale index — if the E1234 chunk was never indexed, no fusion method will surface it
Naively averaging raw BM25 + cosine scores instead of using RRF (or a trained fusion model) is a common bug: the score scales aren't comparable, so one retriever silently dominates

slides.title: The Core Idea, in One Line
bullets: Vector search and keyword search fail on opposite kinds of queries — one on exact tokens, the other on paraphrase
Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines both retrievers' rankings using only rank position, avoiding the trap of comparing incompatible score scales
Documents both retrievers agree on rise to the top; documents only one likes still get some credit but rank lower — usually exactly the behavior you want

questions.prompt: A user searches for 'error E1234' in a support-doc RAG system. Pure vector search ranks a generic error-handling guide above the one document that literally contains 'E1234'. Why?
options: The vector index is corrupted
Dense embeddings optimize for semantic similarity, and rare tokens like specific IDs are often undertrained, so exact substring matches aren't guaranteed to rank highest
Vector search always ignores numbers
The generic guide is a longer document
questions.explanation: Embeddings compress text into vectors trained for topical/semantic similarity, not exact-string matching. Rare tokens like error codes, SKUs, or IDs are often underrepresented in training data, so their embeddings don't reliably separate from semantically similar but factually different text.

questions.prompt: What does Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) use to combine results from BM25 and vector search?
options: The raw BM25 term-frequency score and the raw cosine similarity, averaged together
Only whichever retriever returns more results
Each retriever's normalized probability distribution
Each document's rank position in each retriever's list, via 1/(k + rank), ignoring the raw scores entirely
questions.explanation: RRF deliberately ignores raw scores because BM25 and cosine similarity live on incompatible scales. By fusing on rank position alone, it avoids needing any score normalization or calibration between retrievers.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a real limitation of hybrid search (BM25 + vector + RRF)?
options: It can recover a relevant chunk that was never indexed in the first place
It requires running and maintaining two separate indexes plus a fusion step, adding infra and latency
It eliminates the need for chunking
It guarantees perfect ranking for every query
questions.explanation: Hybrid search fixes a retrieval-method mismatch (keyword vs. semantic), not indexing or chunking problems — and it costs more to run than either retriever alone, since you're maintaining two indexes plus a fusion step.

posts.title: MCP Sampling: Letting a Server Borrow the Client's LLM
posts.subtitle: The server asks a question; the client decides who answers it
posts.summary: MCP's sampling/createMessage lets a server request an LLM completion without holding its own model or API key — the connected client resolves the model, can insert human approval, and returns just the result. It trades server autonomy for shared cost, consistency, and a real security boundary against prompt injection.

slides.title: An MCP Server Can Ask the Client to Think For It
slides.body: Most MCP servers only do deterministic work — search, read a file, hit an API. Sampling is the one primitive where a server can ask for something more: a piece of actual LLM reasoning, without running a model itself.

slides.title: Servers Calling Their Own LLM Duplicate Keys, Cost, and Trust
bullets: If every MCP server holds its own OpenAI/Anthropic key, one agent session can spin up N separate subscriptions and N separate places a key can leak.
A server calling its own API can't see what model, budget, or safety policy the host application actually wants used.
Without a shared path, servers either skip LLM calls entirely or hardcode a model choice the user never approved.

slides.title: Sampling: the Server Proposes, the Client Disposes
slides.body: MCP's sampling/createMessage request lets a server ask the connected client to run a completion on its behalf — using the client's model access and credentials, not the server's own.
bullets: The server sends messages plus modelPreferences (priorities like cost, speed, intelligence) — never a hardcoded model name.
The client resolves those preferences to an actual model, can show a human the proposed prompt for approval, then runs it.
The server never sees the client's API key and never picks the model directly — it only expresses intent.

slides.title: The Round Trip Has Two Hops, Not One
bullets: Server -> Client: sampling/createMessage (messages, modelPreferences, maxTokens, optional systemPrompt).
Client -> Host LLM: the client resolves modelPreferences to a real model, optionally pauses for human approval, then calls it.
Client -> Server: returns just the generated text (and which model actually ran) as the response.
A human clicking 'approve' sits inside this loop, so a sampling call can stall a tool invocation for as long as that approval takes.

slides.title: A Code-Review Server With No LLM of Its Own
slides.body: Picture an MCP server that exposes a review_diff tool. Instead of calling an LLM API itself, it packages the diff into a sampling request; the client runs it through whatever model the user has configured and hands back a written review.
bullets: The server ships with zero LLM credentials and zero model version to maintain or upgrade.
If the user swaps their host app's default model, every server using sampling benefits immediately — no server redeploy needed.
The client sits in the middle of every call, so it can redact or block sensitive diff contents before they ever reach the model.

slides.title: Sampling Is One of Several Ways a Server Gets Help

rows: No one — server does its own compute
Deterministic actions: search, file I/O, calling an API
Server needs reasoning or generation it can't do itself
No one — client asks the human, not a model
Server is missing a parameter or needs confirmation
Server calls its own LLM API
Server owns its own model/key; no host oversight

slides.title: Sampling Isn't Free: Support, Latency, and Trust Boundaries
slides.body: Sampling gives a server influence over what gets generated, not authority — the client can always refuse, edit, or downgrade the request.
bullets: Not every MCP client implements the sampling capability yet — a server depending on it needs a fallback path, not an assumption.
Because a human may need to approve the prompt first, sampling can be far slower than a direct API call — don't put it in a tight request/response loop.

The server controls what the model sees, so a buggy or malicious server can still attempt prompt injection through the messages it sends — the client's approval step is a real security boundary, not a formality.
Sampling suits open-ended 'help me reason about this' requests; for anything deterministic, a plain tool call is simpler and faster.

questions.prompt: In MCP, who actually chooses which model runs a sampling/createMessage request?
options: The server, since it wrote the prompt
The client, using the server's modelPreferences as a hint
Whichever model is cheapest, automatically, with no input from either side
The end user, who must hardcode it into the server's config file
questions.explanation: modelPreferences (priorities like cost, speed, intelligence) are hints the server includes, but the client resolves them to a concrete model — the server never names a model directly.

questions.prompt: Why can a sampling/createMessage call be much slower than the server just calling an LLM API directly?
options: MCP always batches sampling requests in groups of ten
The client is allowed to insert a human-approval step before running the completion
Sampling requests are retried five times by default
Servers must poll for the result once per second
questions.explanation: Because the client sits between the server and the model, it can pause to show a human the proposed prompt before running it — a safety feature that adds real latency the server can't skip or control.

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between MCP Sampling and MCP Elicitation?
options: They are two names for the exact same feature
Sampling asks the client to run an LLM completion; elicitation asks the client to ask a human for information
Elicitation has been deprecated in favor of sampling
Sampling only works when the client and server are made by the same vendor
questions.explanation: Sampling routes a completion request through the client's LLM; elicitation routes a request for missing information or confirmation to a human — different destinations for 'I need help finishing this.'

posts.title: LoRA: Fine-Tuning Big Models by Training a Tiny Fraction of Weights
posts.subtitle: Freeze the giant matrix, learn a thin detour around it
posts.summary: LoRA fine-tunes huge models by freezing the original weights and training a small low-rank detour matrix instead — cutting trainable parameters by 10,000x with no extra inference cost. QLoRA pushes it further by quantizing the frozen base model to 4-bit, making it possible to fine-tune a 65B model on one GPU.

slides.title: Full fine-tuning of a 175B model needs a 175B-parameter update
slides.body: That's a full duplicate copy of the model's optimizer state per task. LoRA asks: what if the *change* the model needs is much smaller than the model itself?

slides.title: Full fine-tuning doesn't scale past one model, one task
slides.body: Every fine-tuned checkpoint of a 175B-parameter model costs ~350GB to store and needs its own copy of Adam's optimizer state (2x the parameter count) during training.
bullets: Want 20 task-specific versions of GPT-3? That's 20 full 175B-parameter checkpoints.
Switching tasks at serving time means swapping the entire model in and out of GPU memory.
Training itself needs 3-4x the model's memory just for gradients and optimizer state.

slides.title: The weight update ΔW is assumed to have low 'intrinsic rank'
slides.body: Instead of learning a full ΔW the same size as the frozen weight matrix W, LoRA factors it into two small matrices: ΔW = B·A, where B is d×r and A is r×k, with r as small as 4-8.
bullets: W (frozen, pretrained) stays untouched — only B and A are trained.
r (the rank) is tiny compared to d and k — e.g. r=8 vs. d=12,288 in GPT-3.
At inference, W + B·A is merged into one matrix — zero extra latency vs. the base model.

slides.title: GPT-3 175B: 10,000x fewer trainable parameters, 3x less GPU memory
slides.body: In the original LoRA paper (Hu et al., 2021), applying rank-4 LoRA adapters to just the query and value attention projections of GPT-3 matched or beat full fine-tuning on downstream tasks.
bullets: Trainable parameters: ~18M instead of 175B — a 10,000x reduction.
GPU memory during training: cut by roughly 3x since Adam no longer tracks state for frozen weights.
No added inference latency, unlike adapter layers that insert extra sequential computation.

slides.title: QLoRA: quantize the frozen model, keep the adapters in higher precision
slides.body: QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) quantizes the frozen base model to 4-bit (NF4) and backpropagates through it into full-precision LoRA adapters, plus double quantization and paged optimizers to avoid memory spikes.
bullets: Fine-tunes a 65B-parameter model on a single 48GB GPU.
Their Guanaco model reached 99.3% of ChatGPT's quality on the Vicuna benchmark after 24 hours on one GPU.
The frozen 4-bit weights never need gradients — only the small adapters do.

slides.title: Where you put the adapters changes the result

rows: Slightly more headroom on harder tasks
Best quality, closer to full fine-tuning cost

slides.title: Pitfalls: rank too low underfits, merging isn't always free
slides.body: LoRA isn't magic — a rank that's too small caps how much the model can actually learn, and swapping many adapters at serving time (unmerged) adds real latency.
bullets: Rank 4-8 is enough for style/format shifts; deep domain shifts often need r=32-64+.
Keeping adapters unmerged (for multi-tenant serving) reintroduces a small latency cost.
LoRA adapts what the base model already knows — it won't teach genuinely new facts as reliably as continued pretraining.
Not a fit when you need to change the model's tokenizer, architecture, or add new modalities.

questions.prompt: What does LoRA actually train during fine-tuning?
options: The full pretrained weight matrix W
Two small low-rank matrices B and A that approximate the weight update
Only the model's embedding layer
A separate reward model
questions.explanation: LoRA freezes W entirely and learns ΔW ≈ B·A, where B and A are much smaller than W — that's the whole trick behind the parameter savings.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't LoRA add inference latency, unlike adapter layers?
options: It runs on a separate GPU
B·A can be merged directly into W before serving, producing one matrix
It skips the forward pass entirely
It only works during training, never during inference
questions.explanation: Because ΔW = B·A has the same shape as W, you can just compute W_new = W + B·A once and deploy that — no extra sequential layers at inference time.

questions.prompt: What does QLoRA add on top of LoRA?
options: A bigger rank r for every layer
Quantizing the frozen base model to 4-bit while keeping adapters in higher precision
Removing the need for a frozen base model entirely
Training on synthetic data only
questions.explanation: QLoRA's key idea is 4-bit NF4 quantization of the frozen weights plus double quantization and paged optimizers — letting you fine-tune a 65B model on one 48GB GPU.

references.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models (Hu et al., 2021)
QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs (Dettmers et al., 2023)

posts.title: When EOS Tokens Disagree: Why Distilled Models Ramble
posts.subtitle: A student and teacher can agree on the rules and still disagree on when to stop
posts.summary: A September 2026 paper from UNC Chapel Hill, BYU, and Microsoft finds that 'length inflation' in on-policy distillation isn't caused by reward hacking — it's caused by student and teacher models placing their stopping probability on different EOS tokens, even when their declared stop-token sets are identical. Aggregating functionally-equivalent EOS tokens into one shared 'stop' signal substantially reduces the problem.

slides.title: A student model reaches the right answer at token 1,094 — then keeps going for 7,098 more
slides.body: That's the kind of length inflation researchers were seeing in on-policy distillation. The paper traces it to a surprisingly specific cause: which exact token the model uses to say 'stop.'

slides.title: On-policy distillation trains a student on its own generations
slides.body: Unlike classic distillation (train on the teacher's outputs), on-policy distillation (OPD) has the student generate its own responses, then scores them against a stronger teacher model — cheaper and often more effective for reasoning tasks.
bullets: But OPD-trained students frequently balloon in response length, sometimes exhausting the entire generation budget without emitting a stop token.
That's expensive at inference time and can silently truncate otherwise-correct answers.
The paper tests this across three model families: Qwen3, Llama, and Gemma.

slides.title: The real cause: termination-token mismatch, not verbosity
slides.body: Every model has a declared 'stopping set' — the token IDs allowed to end generation. The paper's finding: a base student and its post-trained teacher can have the *same* declared stopping set but place almost all their actual stopping probability on *different* tokens within that set.
bullets: Training nudges the student toward the teacher's preferred continuations token-by-token.
If the teacher rarely uses the student's preferred EOS token, that update quietly erodes the student's own tendency to stop.
The stopping sets matching each other says nothing about where the probability mass actually sits.

slides.title: 1,094 tokens to the right answer, then 7,098 more
slides.body: The paper documents a concrete case on a math reasoning task: the student's response contains the correct final answer at token 1,094, then continues generating redundant content for another 7,098 tokens before hitting the budget limit.
bullets: This isn't rare noise — it's the pattern the paper set out to explain systematically.
It shows up across all three tested model families, not one architecture quirk.
The cost compounds: every redundant token is billed and adds latency at serving time.

slides.title: The fix: treat equivalent EOS tokens as one shared action
slides.body: Simply forcing the student and teacher to declare the same allowed stop-token set isn't enough — the paper shows this directly. What works: aggregating the probabilities of functionally-equivalent EOS tokens into a single 'semantic stopping action' during training.
bullets: This substantially reduces mismatch-induced length inflation across Qwen3, Llama, and Gemma.
The intervention targets the training signal itself, not just decoding-time constraints.
Code implementing the fix was released alongside the paper.

slides.title: Not all fixes address the real cause

rows: Aggregate equivalent EOS tokens into one signal

slides.title: One diagnosed cause, not a full cure
slides.body: The authors are explicit about a limitation: length inflation can reappear later in training even after termination alignment, meaning other, still-unexplained dynamics are also at play.
bullets: Don't treat EOS aggregation as a complete fix for verbose OPD-trained models — verify length behavior late in training too.
If you're building a distillation pipeline, log where stopping probability mass sits, not just whether stop-token sets match.
This is a training-time fix; decoding-time truncation still helps as a safety net regardless.

questions.prompt: What did the paper identify as the main cause of length inflation in on-policy distillation?
options: The teacher model rewards longer answers
Termination-token mismatch: student and teacher put stopping probability on different EOS tokens despite identical stopping sets
The student model has a smaller vocabulary than the teacher
Generation temperature is set too high
questions.explanation: The paper's core finding is that having the same *set* of allowed stop tokens doesn't mean the two models agree on which one to actually use — that mismatch drives the inflation.

questions.prompt: Why is aligning the declared stopping set alone not enough to fix the problem?
options: Because stopping sets can't be aligned technically
Because it doesn't change where the actual stopping probability mass sits between the shared tokens
Because it makes responses too short
Because it only works for Qwen3 models
questions.explanation: The paper shows this experimentally: matching which tokens are allowed to stop doesn't fix the issue if the models still disagree on which of those allowed tokens to actually favor.

questions.prompt: According to the paper's own stated limitation, what is NOT true about the proposed fix?
options: It works across Qwen3, Llama, and Gemma
It substantially reduces length inflation
It permanently eliminates length inflation for the rest of training
It targets training rather than just decoding-time truncation
questions.explanation: The authors note length inflation can reappear later in training even after the fix — it's a substantial mitigation, not a permanent cure.

references.title: When EOS Tokens Disagree: Understanding Length Inflation in On-Policy Distillation

posts.title: GPT-6 Astra: Record Benchmarks, Real Independent-Eval Pushback
posts.subtitle: OpenAI's biggest training run yet ships with a Critical safety rating and a benchmark dispute attached
posts.summary: OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra in early September 2026, claiming saturating scores on FrontierMath Tier 4, ARC-AGI-3, and ExploitBench — and, for the first time, a Critical cybersecurity rating under its own Preparedness Framework. Independent evaluators dispute how clean those numbers are, and Astra roughly ties its own predecessor on a neutral benchmark.

slides.title: OpenAI's largest training run ever, on 100,000+ GPUs at Stargate, Texas
slides.body: GPT-6 Astra rolled out to approved users on September 3, 2026, with general availability the next day. OpenAI calls it 'the world's most intelligent and aligned model.'

slides.title: What OpenAI claims Astra is state-of-the-art at
slides.body: OpenAI positions Astra as state-of-the-art on computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science, and professional work — with better focus on task boundaries and multi-step workflows than prior models.
bullets: Available in ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise plans.
Also shipped via the OpenAI API and through Amazon Web Services.
Marketed as faster and more capable across more tasks than any prior GPT iteration.

slides.title: The headline numbers: three saturated benchmarks
bullets: FrontierMath Tier 4: 98% — OpenAI says it has already helped solve long-standing open math problems.
ExploitBench: 100%.
slides.body: OpenAI describes all three as 'saturated' — meaning the benchmark is close to maxed out for this model, a threshold few prior models reached simultaneously.

slides.title: First model to hit 'Critical' on OpenAI's own Preparedness Framework
slides.body: OpenAI classifies Astra as Critical in cybersecurity capability — the top tier of its internal risk framework — High in biological/chemical capability, and below High in AI self-improvement.
bullets: Advanced cyber capabilities are gated behind OpenAI's 'Daybreak' program rather than shipped openly.
OpenAI has also noted Astra's written chain-of-thought is harder to monitor than prior models, even as it appears more obedient to stated user boundaries.
This is the first time OpenAI has applied its most severe Preparedness Framework tier to a shipped model.

slides.title: Pricing jumped roughly 2.5x over the prior flagship
bullets: For comparison, GPT-5.6 Sol's standard API rate was $4 input / $20 output per million tokens.

slides.title: Independent evaluators aren't fully on board with the headline numbers
slides.body: Epoch AI, which runs FrontierMath, discloses that OpenAI funded its development and has exclusive access to part of the benchmark — and had not independently reproduced the Astra result as of the cutoff.
bullets: On the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Astra scores 61.2 — statistically tied with its own predecessor, GPT-5.6 Sol.
On that same neutral index, Astra trails Claude Fable 5.1, which scores 65.7.
The gap between OpenAI's saturated in-house benchmarks and a flat result on a third-party index is the central tension in Astra's launch.

slides.title: Read frontier benchmark claims against who funded and controls them
slides.body: Astra is a genuinely significant release — the Critical safety classification alone is a first — but its own headline numbers and a neutral third-party index tell different stories.
bullets: A benchmark run by a lab that also funds the evaluator (Epoch AI/FrontierMath) deserves independent corroboration before treating it as settled.
A 'saturated' score can coexist with a flat result on a broader, model-agnostic index like Artificial Analysis.
The Critical cybersecurity rating and gated Daybreak access are the more concrete, verifiable signal here than the raw percentages.
At ~2.5x the API price of its predecessor, evaluate Astra against your actual task, not just the leaderboard screenshot.

posts.title: Context Engineering: Curating What the Model Actually Sees
posts.subtitle: Agents don't fail from too little context — they fail from too much of the wrong context
posts.summary: Context engineering is the practice of actively deciding what goes into an agent's context window at each step, instead of just appending everything. Four core moves — compaction, offloading, just-in-time retrieval, and sub-agent isolation — keep an agent's working context small and relevant even as a task grows, which matters because models attend far better to a short, curated context than to a long one stuffed with stale tool output.

slides.title: Prompt Engineering Wrote the Message. Context Engineering Curates the Whole Window.
slides.body: As agents run longer — calling tools, reading files, chaining subtasks — the hard problem stops being 'what do I say to the model' and becomes 'what does the model see right now, out of everything that has happened so far.' That curation is context engineering.
bullets: Prompt engineering: craft one message
Context engineering: manage an entire, growing working memory

slides.title: More Context Isn't Free — It's a Liability
slides.body: An agent that reads files, calls tools, and searches the web accumulates a transcript where most tokens are stale noise by the time the task finishes. That noise isn't harmless: it costs money and latency, and it actively competes with the tokens that matter.
bullets: 'Lost in the middle': models attend best to the start and end of context, worst to facts buried in the middle of a long transcript
Every extra token is paid for at every subsequent step, not just once
A model can't tell which of 50 old tool outputs is still relevant unless something tells it

slides.title: Four Levers: Compact, Offload, Retrieve Just-in-Time, Isolate
slides.body: None of these require a different model — they're all about what you choose to feed it at each step.
bullets: Compaction: periodically collapse old turns and tool outputs into a short running summary, then drop the raw transcript
Offloading: write large artifacts (diffs, search results, logs) to a file or scratchpad; keep only a reference in the live context
Just-in-time retrieval: fetch the specific chunk or tool result only when it's needed, instead of stuffing everything upfront
Sub-agent isolation: hand a subtask to a subagent with its own fresh context; only its final summary returns to the parent

slides.title: A Concrete Compaction Loop
slides.body: One common implementation: the agent tracks its own context budget and compacts before it ever gets close to full.
bullets: Append each tool call's raw output to a working buffer as it happens
When the buffer nears a set fraction of the context budget (e.g. ~20%), ask the model to compress it into a short structured summary — decisions made, open questions, key facts
Discard the raw buffer; keep the summary plus a pointer to where the full detail was saved
If a later step needs the exact detail again, re-open the saved file rather than trusting a compressed memory of it

slides.title: A Coding Agent: 200 Files Touched, Context Stays Flat
slides.body: An autonomous coding agent is asked to refactor a large repo. Without context engineering, every file read, diff, and test log stays in the transcript — by file 30 the window is dominated by stale diffs, and the agent starts losing track of the original instructions.
bullets: With context engineering, the agent keeps a running plan (a few hundred tokens) plus short per-file summaries
Every diff is written to disk immediately; the transcript keeps only the file path and a one-line result
Need the exact code again? Re-read the file from disk — cheap and exact — instead of relying on a fuzzy memory of it
Result: context size stays roughly flat even after touching 200 files, because the filesystem is the source of truth, not the transcript

slides.title: Stuff-Everything vs. Context-Engineered

rows: Forgets early instructions; reasons from stale data
Can lose a detail if compaction is too aggressive
Scan the entire history and hope it's there
Re-fetch the specific artifact by its saved reference

slides.title: When Context Engineering Backfires
slides.body: Every lever above trades something away, and the tradeoff is invisible until it fails.
bullets: Over-compaction can silently drop a constraint the model needed 10 steps later — the failure only shows up as a wrong later action, far from its cause
Sub-agent isolation adds real coordination overhead (extra tokens and round-trips to delegate and merge); it only pays off when the subtask is genuinely separable
Just-in-time retrieval trades recall for precision — if the retrieval step misses the right chunk, the agent never sees it at all, whereas 'stuff everything' at least had it somewhere
Rule of thumb: add these levers once context bloat is causing measurable failures or cost, not preemptively for a short, single-turn task

slides.title: Treat the Context Window Like Working Memory, Not a Log
slides.body: The context window is the model's entire working memory for that step — every token in it is competing for attention, and every token left out is a fact the model can't use.
bullets: Context engineering = actively deciding what the model sees at each step, not appending everything and hoping
Four core moves: compact, offload, retrieve just-in-time, isolate into subagents
External storage (a file, a database) is more reliable long-term memory than the transcript itself
Start simple — add these levers only once context bloat is an observed problem

questions.prompt: What does "lost in the middle" describe?
options: Models run out of GPU memory once context gets too long
Models attend well to the start and end of a long context but poorly to information buried in the middle
A tokenizer bug that drops the middle third of a document
Agents forgetting their goal after a system restart
questions.explanation: It's a measured attention pattern: LLMs use facts near the beginning or end of a long context far more reliably than facts placed in the middle — so simply appending everything to context doesn't guarantee the model will actually use it.

questions.prompt: In the four-levers framework, what does "offloading" mean?
options: Permanently deleting old context so it can never be recovered
Writing large intermediate artifacts to storage and keeping only a reference or short summary in the live context
Sending context to a smaller, cheaper model to process instead
Splitting one prompt across several parallel model calls
questions.explanation: Offloading keeps the live context small by moving bulky raw data — full file contents, tool logs — out to external storage, retrievable by reference whenever the agent actually needs the full detail again.

questions.prompt: Per the pitfalls slide, why doesn't sub-agent isolation always pay off?
options: Subagents can't call tools, only the parent agent can
Spinning up and coordinating a subagent adds its own token and latency overhead, which only pays off when the subtask is genuinely separable
Subagents share the exact same context window as the parent, so nothing is actually isolated
Subagents are always restricted to a less capable model
questions.explanation: Delegating to a subagent costs extra round-trips and tokens to hand off the subtask and merge its result back — worthwhile only when the subtask's own context genuinely shouldn't pollute the parent's.

posts.title: Grouped-Query Attention: Splitting Heads to Save Memory
posts.subtitle: Llama 2, Mistral, and Llama 3 all quietly share one trick: fewer K/V heads than query heads.
posts.summary: Grouped-Query Attention shares each Key/Value head across a group of Query heads instead of giving every head its own — shrinking the KV cache by 4-8x with almost none of the quality loss that plain Multi-Query Attention takes. It's why Llama 2 70B, Mistral 7B, and Llama 3 all serve at a fraction of the memory a full multi-head model would need.

slides.title: The Part of an LLM That Runs Out of Memory First
slides.body: It's rarely the model weights that blow up GPU memory during serving — it's the KV cache, the running record of every token's Key and Value vectors that attention needs to look back on.
bullets: A 70B model's weights are a fixed cost; the KV cache grows with every token you generate and every request you batch
Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) is the architecture change that made long-context, high-batch serving affordable

slides.title: Multi-Head Attention Pays for a K/V Head It Barely Uses
slides.body: Standard multi-head attention (MHA) gives every query head its own private Key and Value projections. That's a lot of redundant state to keep in memory during autoregressive decoding.
bullets: Llama-2-70B has 64 attention heads — full MHA would mean 64 separate K and 64 separate V vectors cached per token, per layer
KV cache size scales as (batch size) × (sequence length) × (num KV heads) × (head dim) × (layers) × 2 — every one of those factors compounds
At long context or large batch, the KV cache can dwarf the model weights themselves, capping how many requests fit on a GPU

slides.title: Share K/V Heads Across Groups of Query Heads
slides.body: Multi-Query Attention (MQA, Shazeer 2019) went to the extreme: every query head shares ONE K/V head. Cache shrinks massively, but quality drops and training gets less stable. GQA (Ainslie et al., 2023) is the tunable middle ground.
bullets: Query heads are split into G groups; every head inside a group shares a single K and V projection
G = number of heads recovers plain MHA exactly; G = 1 recovers MQA exactly — GQA is a dial, not a new mechanism
Existing MHA checkpoints can be converted via 'uptraining': mean-pool the K/V heads within each target group, then continue pretraining for roughly 5% of the original compute to recover quality

slides.title: Why the Extra Compute Is Nearly Free
slides.body: Cutting K/V heads doesn't cut the number of query heads, so the model's representational capacity for 'what to attend to' is untouched — only the K/V projections and the cache they populate shrink.
bullets: The expensive part of decoding is memory bandwidth (streaming the KV cache from HBM), not FLOPs — GQA directly attacks the bottleneck that matters at inference time
Fewer K/V projection matrices also means fewer parameters to store and load, a small win on top of the cache savings
Because grouped heads still each get their own query projection, GQA loses far less expressive power than collapsing to a single shared head (MQA)

slides.title: MHA vs. GQA vs. MQA, in Real Models
bullets: GQA sits deliberately close to MQA's memory savings while staying close to MHA's quality — that's the entire design goal
The right number of KV heads (8 in both examples above) is a hyperparameter choice, not a fixed rule

slides.title: Worked Example: What 8x Smaller Actually Buys You
slides.body: Take a 70B-class model serving a 32K-token context. With full MHA (64 KV heads), the KV cache for that one sequence would need to store 64 K/V pairs per layer, per token.
bullets: Switch to GQA with 8 KV heads and the exact same request needs only 1/8th the KV memory — an 8x reduction with no change to context length or batch size
That freed memory converts directly into serving more concurrent requests (bigger batches) on the same GPU, which is the whole economic point of GQA in production
This is a pure memory win at inference; it does nothing to speed up the one-time prefill pass, which is compute-bound, not bandwidth-bound

slides.title: When GQA Isn't the Right Knob
slides.body: GQA is close to a free lunch, but it's not literally free, and it doesn't solve every memory problem.
bullets: Retrofitting GQA onto an already-trained MHA model still costs real compute (uptraining) — you can't just delete K/V heads at inference and expect the same quality
Pushing G too low still measurably hurts quality on tasks that need fine-grained, per-head specialization, same failure mode as MQA just less severe
GQA shrinks the KV cache, not the model weights — for a memory budget dominated by weights (small models, short context), techniques like quantization matter more
For genuinely extreme memory constraints (edge devices, huge batch serving), MQA or newer compressed-cache methods like MLA can still beat GQA on raw footprint

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: The KV cache, not the model weights, is usually the memory bottleneck when serving LLMs at scale
GQA groups query heads so they share K/V projections — a tunable point between full MHA (best quality) and MQA (smallest cache)
Llama-2-70B (8 KV heads / 64 query heads) and Mistral-7B (8 KV heads / 32 query heads) both ship with GQA today
It's a decode-time memory win, not a prefill speedup — and it still needs uptraining compute if retrofit onto an MHA checkpoint

questions.prompt: What does Grouped-Query Attention actually share to shrink the KV cache?
options: Query projections across all layers
Key and Value projections across a group of query heads
The embedding table across attention heads
A single low-rank compressed cache, as in MLA
questions.explanation: GQA splits query heads into groups and has every head in a group share one Key and one Value projection. Compressing the cache with a shared low-rank representation is the (different) idea behind MLA, not GQA.

questions.prompt: Llama-2-70B has 64 query heads. How many KV heads does its GQA setup use, and what does that give you?
options: 64 KV heads — identical to plain multi-head attention
1 KV head — the same cache size as Multi-Query Attention
8 KV heads — an 8x smaller KV cache than full multi-head attention
32 KV heads — a 2x smaller KV cache
questions.explanation: Llama-2-70B groups its 64 query heads into 8 groups, each sharing one KV head — an 8x reduction in KV cache size versus giving every query head its own K/V pair.

questions.prompt: Why does GQA mainly help decoding rather than the initial prefill pass?
options: Prefill doesn't use attention at all
Decoding is bottlenecked by streaming the KV cache from memory, which GQA shrinks; prefill is compute-bound instead
GQA only activates after the first 1,000 tokens
Prefill already uses a different, cheaper attention mechanism
questions.explanation: Autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth bound — every step re-reads the whole KV cache — so shrinking that cache directly speeds it up. Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel and is limited by compute (FLOPs), not by KV cache size.

references.title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints (Ainslie et al., 2023)

posts.title: Agent Memory: Giving LLM Agents a Memory Beyond the Prompt
posts.subtitle: The context window is working memory, not storage — long-running agents need somewhere to put what they've learned.
posts.summary: A context window is per-session working memory: whatever it holds disappears when the session ends or the window fills up. Production agents that need to persist knowledge across sessions split memory into tiers — working memory in the live context, episodic memory as a searchable log of past interactions, and semantic memory as distilled facts — each with different lifespans, retrieval methods, and risks.

slides.title: Agents Forget Everything When the Context Window Closes
slides.body: A context window is not a memory system — it's scratch space that gets thrown away the moment a session ends, crashes, or gets truncated.
bullets: Every tool call and its result gets appended to context — a 50-step agent loop can burn well over 100K tokens before finishing
Restart the process (new session, deploy, crash) and everything the agent learned along the way is gone
Real agents need memory that survives past a single run, without just growing the context window forever

slides.title: Bigger Context Windows Don't Fix This
slides.body: Just stuffing more history into the prompt runs into cost, latency, and attention limits before it runs into a token cap.
bullets: Long contexts suffer 'lost in the middle': models attend more reliably to the start and end of a prompt than to content buried in the middle
Every extra token of history is re-processed (and re-billed) on every single turn, even the parts that are no longer relevant
A context window that keeps growing across a long-running agent eventually pushes out the system prompt, tool schemas, or the actual task — the things that matter most

slides.title: Three Memory Tiers, Each With a Different Job
slides.body: Systems like MemGPT/Letta popularized treating the context window as 'RAM' and an external store as 'disk' — the agent explicitly decides what to page in and out.
bullets: Working memory: the live context window itself — the current task's scratchpad and recent tool outputs, gone when the session ends
Episodic memory: a log of past interactions stored in a vector DB, pulled back in by similarity search when a new situation resembles an old one
Semantic memory: distilled, structured facts extracted from episodes ('this repo uses pytest') — small, curated, and cheap to inject directly at session start

slides.title: Worked Example: A Coding Agent Across Three Sessions
slides.body: The payoff of tiered memory shows up the second time an agent touches the same codebase, not the first.
bullets: Session 1: the agent discovers the repo uses pytest, not unittest, after one failed test run — it writes that fact to semantic memory
Session 2 (new context, days later): the agent retrieves 'uses pytest' before writing a new test file, skipping the failure it hit last time
Without memory, session 2 re-discovers the same fact by trial and error — the same failed run, the same fix, every single session

slides.title: Working vs. Episodic vs. Semantic Memory

rows: Always in view, no retrieval needed
Similarity search, pulled in on demand
Direct lookup, often injected at session start

slides.title: When Memory Makes Agents Worse
slides.body: Adding memory trades one failure mode (forgetting) for a different set of failure modes if it isn't managed carefully.
bullets: Stale memory: a fact learned months ago ('use Python 3.9') can silently mislead an agent working in a codebase that has since moved to 3.12
Retrieval noise: pulling in the top-10 'similar' memories can inject irrelevant context that hurts reasoning more than the missing context would have

Unbounded write access: an agent that can freely write to its own long-term memory can also have that memory poisoned — a prompt injection that persists an attacker's instruction across every future session

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: A context window is working memory only — treat it as scratch space, not storage
Split persistent memory by lifespan: episodic (raw, searchable) for 'what happened' vs. semantic (distilled, curated) for 'what's true'
Memory writes deserve the same scrutiny as memory reads — an agent that can write to long-term memory can also poison it
Start simple: a single curated facts file re-injected at session start beats an over-engineered vector store for most agents

questions.prompt: Why is a large context window not a substitute for long-term memory in an agent?
options: It resets or gets truncated between sessions, so nothing in it survives past the current run
It's too slow for the agent to read from
It costs the same to process no matter how long it gets
Models can't read more than 4,000 tokens of context
questions.explanation: Context windows are per-session working memory; whatever they hold disappears when the session ends, crashes, or gets truncated — which is exactly the gap long-term memory tiers are built to fill.

questions.prompt: What's the key structural difference between episodic and semantic memory in an agent architecture?
options: Episodic memory is always faster to query than semantic memory
Episodic memory stores raw past interactions for similarity retrieval; semantic memory stores distilled, structured facts
Semantic memory only works with certain model providers
They're the same mechanism with different names
questions.explanation: Episodic memory is closer to a searchable transcript log pulled in by similarity search; semantic memory is curated knowledge already extracted from those transcripts, so it's smaller and reliable enough to inject directly into a prompt.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of letting an agent freely write to its own long-term memory?
options: It consumes more storage than expected
A bad or manipulated memory (e.g. via prompt injection) can persist and silently corrupt every future session
It makes each individual response slower to generate
It forces the agent to use a bigger context window
questions.explanation: Unlike a single bad response that's forgotten once the session ends, a poisoned long-term memory keeps re-injecting itself into every future interaction until someone notices and corrects it — turning a one-time mistake into a standing liability.

posts.title: PagedAttention: The KV Cache as Virtual Memory
posts.subtitle: vLLM borrows a 1960s OS trick to stop LLM servers from reserving gigabytes they'll never use.
posts.summary: PagedAttention (the idea behind vLLM) splits each request's KV cache into fixed-size blocks stored non-contiguously in GPU memory, addressed through a per-sequence block table — exactly like OS virtual memory pages. That single change removes the need to reserve worst-case memory per request, lets identical prefixes share blocks via copy-on-write, and is why modern LLM servers can pack far more concurrent requests onto the same GPU.

slides.title: The KV Cache Problem Nobody Optimizes
slides.body: Every token an LLM generates needs its key/value vectors kept around for every future attention step. That cache grows linearly with sequence length and, in most serving systems, wastes most of the memory it reserves.
bullets: The original PagedAttention paper (Kwon et al., 2023, UC Berkeley) found existing serving systems wasting the majority of their KV cache memory to fragmentation and over-reservation
vLLM built around this idea and became the reference implementation most production LLM servers now imitate

slides.title: Naive Allocation Reserves for the Worst Case
slides.body: A server can't know in advance how many tokens a request will generate, so a naive contiguous allocator reserves memory for the maximum possible sequence length the moment a request arrives.
bullets: Internal fragmentation: a request that stops at 200 tokens still holds its full 2048-token reservation for its entire lifetime — the unused tail is dead weight
External fragmentation: variable-length reservations packed side-by-side in memory leave gaps too small for the next request, just like a fragmented disk
No sharing: beam search or parallel sampling from one prompt duplicates that prompt's entire KV cache once per candidate, even though the candidates start identical

slides.title: Treat the Cache Like OS Virtual Memory
slides.body: PagedAttention splits each sequence's KV cache into fixed-size blocks (16 tokens by default in vLLM) that live non-contiguously in GPU memory, allocated on demand as generation proceeds rather than reserved upfront.
bullets: Each sequence keeps a block table mapping logical block index -> physical block address, the same abstraction an OS page table uses for virtual-to-physical memory
Blocks are handed out one at a time as the sequence grows, so a request that finishes early simply stops requesting new blocks
The attention kernel gathers the correct physical blocks through the table at compute time — the math is identical to a contiguous cache, only the addressing changed

slides.title: Copy-on-Write Lets Requests Share a Prefix
slides.body: When multiple sequences share an identical prefix — a system prompt, or the shared input in beam search and parallel sampling — their block tables can point at the exact same physical blocks.
bullets: Every physical block carries a reference count of how many logical block tables point at it
A shared block stays shared until one sequence needs to write a new, divergent token into it — only then does that sequence get its own private copy (classic copy-on-write, borrowed from OS design)
This is why sampling n candidates from one prompt in vLLM costs close to 1x the prompt's KV memory, not n times

slides.title: Paged vs. Contiguous KV Cache

rows: grown block-by-block as tokens are generated
internal + external, reported as the majority of memory in early serving systems
bounded to under one block's worth per sequence
Reported throughput gain (vLLM paper vs. then-SOTA serving)
2-4x at the same latency, per the original paper

slides.title: Worked Example: 100 Concurrent Requests on One GPU
slides.body: Say a request's KV cache costs roughly 1MB per token (varies by model size and head count). A server that reserves 2048 tokens per request for 100 concurrent requests locks up close to 200GB no matter how many tokens actually get generated.
bullets: With 16-token blocks, a request that only ever generates 200 tokens allocates about 13 blocks (208 slots) instead of a fixed 2048-slot reservation
The memory that would've sat idle in the unused reservation gets handed to other requests' block tables instead
More reclaimed memory means the scheduler can admit more sequences into each batch — that's the actual source of the throughput gain, not a faster attention kernel

slides.title: Where Paging Costs Something — and Where It Doesn't Help
slides.body: Paging isn't free, and it isn't universally useful. Knowing its limits matters as much as knowing the mechanism.
bullets: Every attention step now does an extra indirection: a block-table lookup plus a non-contiguous gather, instead of one contiguous read — a small but real per-step overhead
Block size is a tuning knob: smaller blocks shrink internal fragmentation further but add more per-block bookkeeping; vLLM's default of 16 tokens balances the two
Low-concurrency, single-request deployments see little benefit — the win comes from packing many concurrent sequences tightly, so it matters most under real serving load
Copy-on-write sharing only pays off when sequences actually share a prefix; fully distinct prompts get zero sharing benefit

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: PagedAttention borrows OS virtual memory paging: fixed-size KV cache blocks, a per-sequence block table, and copy-on-write sharing
It changes how K/V tensors are stored and addressed in GPU memory — not the attention math itself
The payoff is a higher achievable batch size: more concurrent sequences fit in the same GPU memory once reservations stop being worst-case
It's the core idea behind vLLM, and the reason most production LLM servers (TensorRT-LLM, TGI, SGLang) now implement some form of paged KV cache management

questions.prompt: What does PagedAttention actually change about how attention is computed?
options: It changes the attention formula to reduce FLOPs
It changes only how the K/V cache is stored and addressed in memory, not the underlying math
It removes the need for a KV cache entirely
It compresses K/V vectors to a lower precision
questions.explanation: PagedAttention is a memory-management technique, not a new attention algorithm — the kernel still computes the same dot products, just gathering K/V from non-contiguous physical blocks via a block table instead of one contiguous buffer. (Contrast with FlashAttention, which changes the compute pattern itself.)

questions.prompt: Why does naive contiguous KV cache allocation waste so much memory?
options: GPUs have too little memory to fit any large cache
It has to reserve space for the maximum possible sequence length upfront, before knowing how many tokens will actually be generated
It stores keys and values in duplicate for safety
It always uses full 32-bit precision for the cache
questions.explanation: Since the eventual output length is unknown when a request starts, a contiguous allocator reserves worst-case space per request. Most requests finish well short of that limit, and the reserved-but-unused tail sits idle for the request's whole lifetime.

questions.prompt: What lets vLLM serve parallel sampling or beam search cheaply?
options: Running each candidate on a separate GPU
Quantizing the KV cache to int8
Copy-on-write sharing of physical blocks across sequences that share a prefix
Skipping attention for repeated tokens
questions.explanation: Candidates that share an identical prefix (the same prompt) point their block tables at the same physical blocks. A private copy is only made once a candidate needs to write a new, divergent token — so n candidates cost close to 1x the prompt's memory, not n times.

posts.title: RoPE: Teaching Attention Where Tokens Are
posts.subtitle: Rotary embeddings encode position as a rotation, not an addition — which is why the math falls out so cleanly.
posts.summary: RoPE rotates each query/key vector by an angle proportional to its position, so the attention dot product depends only on relative distance between tokens. That single design choice is why most modern LLMs (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek) use it instead of learned or sinusoidal position embeddings — and why long-context extension techniques like NTK scaling and YaRN exist to patch its one real weakness.

slides.title: Attention Has No Sense of Order
slides.body: Self-attention computes a weighted sum over all tokens at once — shuffle the input and the raw dot products don't change. Every transformer needs some extra signal to tell 'token 3' apart from 'token 30'.
bullets: Attention(Q,K,V) is permutation-invariant by construction
Position has to be injected some other way — RoPE is the dominant answer in 2024+ open models

slides.title: Adding a Position Vector Doesn't Generalize
slides.body: The original fixes — GPT-2's learned position embeddings, the original Transformer's sinusoidal embeddings — both add a position signal directly to the token embedding before the first layer.
bullets: Learned embeddings: one vector per position index, capped at the trained context length — position 4096 simply doesn't exist if training stopped at 4096
Sinusoidal: extends to unseen lengths in theory, but the model never trained on those magnitudes, so quality degrades fast
Both bake position into the value itself, so the model has to learn relative distance indirectly through many layers

slides.title: Rotate the Vector Instead of Shifting It
slides.body: RoPE (Su et al., 2021, RoFormer) never touches the token embedding. Instead, right before the attention dot product, it rotates each query and key vector by an angle that grows with position.
bullets: Split each d-dimensional Q/K vector into d/2 pairs of coordinates, treat each pair as a 2D point
Rotate pair i at token position m by angle m·θ_i, where θ_i = base^(−2i/d) (base is usually 10000, though Llama 3 raises it to 500000 for long context)
The token's meaning (embedding) is unchanged — only its 'phase' in each frequency band shifts with position

slides.title: Why the Dot Product Only Sees Relative Distance
slides.body: Rotation matrices compose: rotating by m then measuring against a vector rotated by n is mathematically identical to measuring against an unrotated vector rotated by (n−m). Applied to attention, this falls straight out of the algebra.
bullets: q_m · k_n after rotation = a function of (m − n) alone, never of m or n individually
That's the whole payoff: relative position is built into the score, not learned from data
Low-frequency pairs (small θ_i) rotate slowly → encode long-range position; high-frequency pairs rotate fast → encode fine local order

slides.title: Worked Example: Two Tokens, One Frequency Band
slides.body: Take one 2D pair with θ = 0.01 rad/position. A token at position 5 rotates that pair by 0.05 rad; a token at position 12 rotates it by 0.12 rad.
bullets: Their dot product depends only on the angle difference: 0.12 − 0.05 = 0.07 rad
Move both tokens forward by 100 positions (105 and 112) and the angle difference is still exactly 0.07 rad — the score is unchanged
That shift-invariance is exactly what lets attention generalize 'the token 7 steps back' regardless of where in the sequence it happens

slides.title: RoPE vs. the Alternatives

rows: Better, but still degrades without scaling tricks

slides.title: Where RoPE Still Breaks: Long-Context Extension
slides.body: RoPE generalizes better than absolute embeddings, but a model trained at a 4K context still sees rotation angles it never encountered when you feed it 32K tokens — quality degrades past the trained length.
bullets: Position Interpolation (Chen et al., 2023): compress far-away position ids so they stay inside the trained range
NTK-aware scaling: stretch the base frequency instead of the raw positions, preserving high-frequency (local) resolution
YaRN (Peng et al., 2023): blends interpolation and extrapolation per-frequency-band, plus a small amount of continued fine-tuning
None of these are free — they're patches on a real limitation, not a solved problem

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: RoPE encodes position as a rotation applied to Q/K at attention time, not as something added to the embedding
Its dot product depends only on relative distance — the key property that makes it generalize better than absolute schemes
It's now the default in Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, and most open decoder-only LLMs
It still needs help (interpolation, NTK scaling, YaRN) to extend cleanly past its trained context length

questions.prompt: In RoPE, what determines the angle a 2D coordinate pair is rotated by?
options: The token's position multiplied by that pair's frequency θ_i
The number of attention heads in the layer
The token's vocabulary index
The transformer's layer depth
questions.explanation: Each pair i is rotated by angle m·θ_i, where m is the token's position and θ_i = base^(−2i/d) — a different frequency per pair, exactly like the frequency bands in sinusoidal encoding.

questions.prompt: Why does the attention score between two RoPE-rotated vectors depend only on relative position, not absolute position?
options: RoPE clips position ids before rotating
Rotation matrices compose, so R(m)ᵀR(n) reduces to R(n − m) inside the dot product
RoPE normalizes every vector to unit length first
RoPE adds an explicit (m − n) bias term to the attention score
questions.explanation: This is the core algebraic trick: because rotations compose predictably, the dot product of two rotated vectors is a function purely of the angle difference — i.e., of (m − n).

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a real technique for extending a RoPE model's context window past its trained length?
options: Position Interpolation
NTK-aware frequency scaling
YaRN
Raising the softmax temperature during inference
questions.explanation: Softmax temperature controls output randomness, not positional generalization — it does nothing to fix RoPE's extrapolation gap. Interpolation, NTK scaling, and YaRN all specifically rescale position/frequency to stay within (or gracefully extend beyond) the trained range.

posts.title: Encoder-Decoder vs. Decoder-Only: Why Most LLMs Picked One
posts.subtitle: GPT dropped the encoder a decade ago. DeepSeek just shipped a new encoder-decoder family in 2026 — here's the actual tradeoff.
posts.summary: The original Transformer had two halves: an encoder that reads the whole input at once, and a decoder that generates output one token at a time. Most modern LLMs threw the encoder away — but the tradeoff it made never disappeared, and some new models are bringing it back.

slides.title: The Transformer used to have two halves
slides.body: Before GPT made 'decoder-only' the default, the original 2017 Transformer split the work: one stack to read, one stack to write.

slides.title: Encoder: read everything, all at once
slides.body: In the original Transformer (and later T5, BART), the encoder sees the full input sequence simultaneously and attends to it bidirectionally — token 3 can look at token 9 just as easily as token 1. It compresses the whole input into a set of contextual representations before generation ever starts.
bullets: Bidirectional self-attention over the full input
Runs once per input, not once per output token
Produces a fixed set of representations the decoder reads from

slides.title: Decoder: generate one token at a time, looking back
slides.body: The decoder attends only to tokens already generated (causal/masked attention) plus, in the original design, cross-attends into the encoder's output. Strip the encoder out and cross-attention out, and you get exactly the decoder-only architecture GPT popularized: one stack, trained to predict the next token over everything — prompt and answer alike.
bullets: Causal (left-to-right) self-attention only
Decoder-only = no separate encoder, no cross-attention
Same stack handles 'reading' the prompt and 'writing' the answer

slides.title: Why the field mostly went decoder-only
slides.body: Decoder-only won for scaling and generality, not because encoders were 'wrong.'

rows: Simple next-token prediction on raw text

slides.title: Where the split still shows up in 2026
slides.body: DeepSeek's new V4.1-Flash architecture family is described as a 'Causal Encoder-Decoder': a 552B-parameter backbone that activates only 8B parameters per token at prefill (reading your prompt) versus 16B at decode (generating the answer) — separate compute budgets for reading versus writing, the same split the original encoder-decoder made explicit, just implemented with sparse activation instead of two fully separate stacks.
bullets: Prefill (read the prompt) and decode (generate the answer) get different active-parameter budgets
This is only visible because the model separates 'input processing' from 'output generation' internally
A pure decoder-only model treats every position, prompt or answer, identically

slides.title: When encoder-decoder is the wrong choice
slides.body: Two stacks means two things to train, more total parameters for a given capability level, and a fixed encoder representation that's awkward for open-ended, multi-turn conversation where 'the input' keeps growing. That's exactly the gap decoder-only chat models were built to fill.
bullets: Don't reach for encoder-decoder for open-ended chat or agentic multi-turn use
Two-stack training is more complex to scale than one autoregressive stack
Best fit: tasks with a clean, fixed input and a bounded output (translation, summarization, structured extraction)

slides.title: The split never went away — it just went internal
slides.body: Decoder-only won the popularity contest because one stack, one objective, scales more predictably. But the underlying tradeoff — cheap bidirectional reading vs. causal writing — resurfaces whenever a model needs to treat 'understanding the prompt' and 'generating the answer' as different jobs.
bullets: Decoder-only: simplicity and scaling won out for general-purpose chat/agents
Encoder-decoder: still strong for fixed input→output tasks
2026 architectures are reviving the read/write split inside a single model via different active-parameter budgets

questions.prompt: What's the key attention difference between an encoder and a decoder in the original Transformer?
options: The encoder uses causal attention, the decoder uses bidirectional attention
The encoder attends bidirectionally over the full input; the decoder uses causal (left-to-right) attention
They use identical attention patterns
Neither uses self-attention
questions.explanation: The encoder can look at the whole input at once in both directions, since it isn't generating anything. The decoder can only look backward at tokens already produced, because at generation time future tokens don't exist yet.

questions.prompt: Why did most modern LLMs (GPT, Llama) go decoder-only instead of encoder-decoder?
options: Encoders were found to be mathematically incorrect
One stack with a simple next-token objective scales more predictably and handles open-ended generation better than two specialized stacks
Decoder-only models can't use attention at all
Encoder-decoder models can't be trained on text
questions.explanation: Decoder-only models train on a single, simple objective (predict the next token) across all text, which scales cleanly and naturally supports open-ended, multi-turn generation — the two things classic encoder-decoder setups weren't optimized for.

questions.prompt: In DeepSeek's V4.1-Flash 'Causal Encoder-Decoder' family, what differs between prefill and decode?
options: Nothing — they use identical compute
Prefill activates 8B parameters per token, decode activates 16B — separate budgets for reading the prompt vs. generating the answer
Prefill uses no parameters at all
Decode never happens in this architecture
questions.explanation: The 552B-parameter backbone activates 8B parameters per token while processing (reading) the prompt during prefill, and 16B per token while generating (writing) during decode — echoing the classic encoder/decoder division of labor inside one model.

posts.title: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: New Encoder-Decoder Family, Old Model Retired

It posts sharp gains over the prior V4 Flash on coding and reasoning benchmarks, and DeepSeek is routing V4 Pro traffic onto it while it decides V4 Pro's future.

slides.title: DeepSeek retires its own flagship Flash model — for a smaller one
slides.body: V4.1-Flash isn't a bigger model. It's a new architecture family, and it just replaced V4 Flash across the board.

slides.title: Flash models exist to make frontier capability affordable
slides.body: DeepSeek's 'Flash' line trades some raw capability for speed and price, competing on cost-per-token against every other lab's cheap tier. The previous V4 Flash (0731) was already fast — V4.1-Flash had to beat it on both price and quality to be worth shipping.
bullets: Flash tier = lower cost, higher throughput, still agentic-coding capable
Old model: V4 Flash (0731 build)
New model had to win on architecture, not just scale

slides.title: A new 'Causal Encoder-Decoder' family

posts.title: Coding Agents Have Converged: SWE-bench Can't Rank Them
posts.subtitle: A 254-submission audit finds the top two SWE-bench Verified entries tied at 396/500 — the leaderboard order is noise.
posts.summary: A new audit of 254 SWE-bench submissions shows the top coding agents solve almost the same subset of tasks, so tiny score gaps on the leaderboard don't mean one system is actually better. The authors argue for reporting solved-instance overlap and scaffold-controlled ranges instead of a single ordered list.

slides.title: The SWE-bench leaderboard can't order its own top ten
slides.body: An audit of 254 real submissions finds the top coding agents aren't ranked by skill — they're ranked by noise.

slides.title: Every fraction of a point gets read as 'state of the art'
slides.body: SWE-bench Verified scores agents on 500 real GitHub issues. Labs and leaderboards treat a 0.5-point gap between rank #1 and rank #4 as proof one system is better engineered — without checking whether they're actually solving different problems.
bullets: 500-instance Verified split is the reference benchmark for coding-agent quality
Leaderboards rank by aggregate resolve-rate to one decimal place
No standard check for whether top entries solve the *same* instances

slides.title: Audit the submissions, don't rerun the models
slides.body: Researchers from Imperial College London, HK PolyU, Korea University, and Jinan University pulled 254 real SWE-bench leaderboard submissions across four splits and compared which instances each agent actually resolved — no re-running required.
bullets: 254 submissions audited across 4 SWE-bench splits
Measured per-instance overlap ('nesting') between top solution sets
Compared score-implied independence vs. actual shared successes

slides.title: The numbers behind 'converged'
slides.body: Frontier agents aren't spreading out across different problems — they're clustering on the same ones.

rows: Share 285 successes + 51 failures — only 164 instances actually distinguish them

slides.title: A 29.8-point swing that has nothing to do with the model
slides.body: The audit found cases where the exact same underlying model scored wildly differently just by swapping the agent scaffold around it — a 29.8-point range. Compare that to the 8.8-point gap separating the entire top thirty on the leaderboard: scaffold choice alone can move a system further than three-quarters of the leaderboard's real spread.
bullets: Same model + different harness = up to 29.8-point score change
Entire top-30 leaderboard spans only 8.8 points
A leaderboard rank can reflect scaffold engineering, not model capability

slides.title: What to measure instead of a single rank
slides.body: The authors argue single-number leaderboard rankings overstate precision the data can't support, and propose reporting overlap and tiers instead.
bullets: Report solved-instance overlap between top systems, not just aggregate score
Group systems into statistical tiers instead of a strict 1-to-N order

posts.title: PhysBrain 1.5: A VLM That Predicts Its Own Next Frame
posts.subtitle: One autoregressive backbone that perceives a scene, picks an action, and imagines what happens next.
posts.summary: PhysBrain 1.5 extends Qwen3-VL into a unified backbone that jointly outputs language, robot actions, and predicted future visual states as one token stream. Its 8B model averages 72.5 across 28 embodied benchmarks, ranking first on 14 of them and landing near proprietary frontier models like GPT-6 Astra.

slides.title: Perception, action, and prediction — one backbone, one token stream
slides.body: PhysBrain 1.5 (arXiv 2609.14973) turns a general vision-language model into what its authors call a physical foundation model.
bullets: Built on Qwen3-VL
Two sizes: 2B and 8B parameters
8B: 72.5 average across 28 embodied benchmarks

slides.title: Robots need three models that don't talk to each other
slides.body: Typical embodied stacks bolt together a perception model, a policy network, and (sometimes) a separate world model — each trained on different data, each a place for errors to leak between stages.
bullets: A VLM can describe a scene but not output a motor command
A policy network can act but can't explain why, or check its own prediction
A separate world-model needs its own training pipeline and inference pass
Stitching them together adds latency and mismatched representations at every handoff

slides.title: Everything becomes a token, in one autoregressive loop
slides.body: PhysBrain encodes language responses, end-effector motion, and dense visual targets as discrete token sequences, then jointly trains next-token prediction across all three.
bullets: Actions use ActionPiece tokens plus a unified action codebook
Future states are predicted as RGB frames, depth maps, and robot masks — not just text
One shared backbone means perception, control, and prediction share the same representations
The model can be queried for 'what happens if I do X' before ever moving

slides.title: Training recipe: human video first, robots second
slides.body: The hard part of embodied AI is data — real robot trajectories are scarce and expensive. PhysBrain sidesteps this with a two-stage recipe.
bullets: Pretraining: embodied supervision comes entirely from human interaction videos, mined for task-centered episodes
This pairs semantic/spatial context with recovered human motion and what happened next
Fine-tuning: mixes real human demos, real robot trajectories, and simulated experience
Video supervision is what lets an 8B model reach frontier-adjacent scores without a warehouse of robots

slides.title: 8B vs 2B: size still buys you the leaderboard
slides.body: Across 28 embodied-understanding benchmarks, the size gap between checkpoints is stark — and the 2B variant isn't even ranked competitively.

slides.title: Worked example: deciding whether to pour, before pouring
slides.body: Ask PhysBrain to fill a cup from a pitcher and it doesn't just emit a motion trajectory — it can roll the plan forward internally first.
bullets: Perceives the scene: cup position, pitcher tilt angle, liquid level
Proposes an action as ActionPiece tokens for the arm trajectory
Predicts the resulting RGB/depth frame — does the cup look overfilled?
Only then commits to the action, instead of executing blind and correcting after a spill

slides.body: Folding perception, action, and prediction into one token stream is elegant, but it inherits real weaknesses.
bullets: Human-video pretraining has a domain gap: human hands are not robot end-effectors
Predicting future frames adds an extra generation pass per action step — real latency cost
72.5/100 average means it's still wrong on a meaningful share of the 28 benchmarks
The 2B model's exclusion from rankings shows this approach needs scale to be competitive at all

bullets: First open model to seriously close the gap to proprietary systems on embodied benchmarks
Shows action tokens and future-frame prediction can share a backbone with a normal VLM — no separate world model needed
Human-video pretraining is a scalable substitute for scarce real-robot data
The 8B-vs-2B gap is a reminder that 'unified token stream' architectures still obey normal scaling laws
